stories.title: CD73 disruption with tumor-specific CRISPR/Cas9 nanoparticles reduces adenosine-mediated immunosuppression and amplifies response to chemotherapy
stories.description: The therapeutic efficacy of cancer immunotherapy is impaired by poor tumor immunogenicity and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), partially driven by reprogrammed adenosine metabolism in the tumor. Here, we develop degradable CRISPR/Cas9 nanoparticles to durably and precisely downregulate CD73 expression across multiple cell subsets within the tumor microenvironment, including tumor cells, endothelial cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, and tumor-infiltrating immune cells, thereby effectively disrupting adenosine metabolism. In combination with immunogenic cell death induced by the co-delivered chemotherapeutic drug doxorubicin, this strategy synergistically potentiates tumor immunogenicity and reprograms the TME into an immunostimulatory state. This immune remodeling contributes to tumor control, prolonging median survival in preclinical models of melanoma and triple negative breast cancer in female mice. This study provides a strategy for precise and durable regulation of cancer immunometabolism to improve therapeutic effects of chemo-immunotherapy for synergistic cancer therapy. Extracellular adenosine, generated by the hydrolysis of ATP by CD39 and CD73, contributes to immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment (TME). Here the authors report that disruption of CD73 with tumor specific CRISPR/Cas9 nanoparticles reduces adenosine mediated immunosuppression in the TME and amplify response to chemo-immunotherapy.

stories.title: The proapoptotic protein BID is dispensable for establishment of the ovarian reserve and overall fertility in mice
stories.description: The size of the ovarian reserve established during early life is a key determinant of female reproductive lifespan, and is shaped by tightly regulated processes of follicle activation and apoptosis. However, the molecular pathways governing these events remain incompletely defined. BID is a pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein that links extrinsic death receptor signalling to the intrinsic mitochondrial apoptotic pathway, and has been implicated in cell death regulation in multiple tissues. Here, we investigated the role of BID in follicle dynamics and female fertility using Bid−/− mice. Ovaries from wild-type and Bid−/− mice were examined at postnatal day 1 (PN1) PN5, PN10 and PN50. Establishment of the ovarian reserve was not altered by loss of BID, as total germ cell numbers and ovarian morphology were comparable between genotypes. However, Bid−/− mice displayed a transient increase in primordial follicle activation at PN5, characterised by reduced primordial follicle numbers and increased primary follicles, with a corresponding rise in secondary follicles at PN10. This phenotype was not sustained at later stages. In adult ovaries, loss of BID resulted in a reduction in follicular atresia, with decreased numbers of atretic growing follicles and reduced granulosa cell apoptosis as assessed by TUNEL staining. Consistent with altered follicle dynamics, Bid−/− mice exhibited reduced numbers of corpora lutea in vivo. However, exogenous gonadotrophin stimulation revealed no difference in ovulatory capacity between genotypes. Despite these changes, Bid−/− females remained fully fertile, with only slight alterations in time to first litter and litter size, and no difference in cumulative pup output. Together, these findings demonstrate that BID is dispensable for establishment of the ovarian reserve and overall fertility, but contributes to the regulation of follicle activation and survival during postnatal ovarian development.

stories.title: Complete disruption of gD binding to HVEM alters virus replication and host receptor homeostasis
stories.description: Author summary Previously, we demonstrated that loss of HVEM impairs HSV-1 reactivation without significantly affecting primary viral replication. As a member of the TNF receptor superfamily, HVEM functions as a key immunomodulatory receptor and a critical entry mediator for HSV-1 through its interaction with glycoprotein D (gD). Beyond facilitating viral entry, gD–HVEM engagement can influence host immune signaling pathways, thereby shaping the local immune environment during infection. In this study, we identify amino acids 27–29 of gD as essential determinants for HVEM binding. These findings provide mechanistic insight into how HSV-1 exploits specific receptor interactions not only to gain entry but also to modulate immune responses. Disruption of the gD–HVEM interface, therefore, represents a promising strategy to limit viral spread and reactivation while potentially preserving antigen presentation and immune recognition.
